text: Are the leaf spots small, no bigger than a pencil tip or about 1/8 inch, and numerous?

passages.passage: Tomato leaves have small (less than 1/8 inch), brown, circular spots surrounded by a yellow halo.
Septoria is identified as small (1/16” to 1/8”), water-soaked spots on the underside of the leaves initially
circular lesions up to 1/2" in diameter are produced

text: Do the spots have dark rings inside them, like a target or bull's-eye?

passages.passage: The lesions develop a "bulls-eye" pattern of concentric rings that can be seen with a hand lens.
The leaf spots do not contain concentric rings, spots with concentric rings are likely caused by early blight

text: Are the centers of the spots gray or tan-white, with tiny black dots in them when you look through a magnifier?

passages.passage: Mature lesions have a dark margin with a grayish white center that contains tiny, black fruiting (spore-producing) bodies.
Inspecting the center of the spots closely, tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) may be seen with the aid of a hand-held magnifying loupe.

text: Has the middle of some spots dried and dropped out, leaving small holes in the leaf?

passages.passage: The center of the leaf spots often falls out resulting in small holes.

text: Turn a spotted leaf over: is there white, fuzzy or cottony growth on the underside near the spots?

passages.passage: White, fuzzy growth may be found on the undersides of leaves or on lower stems.
During high humidity, white cottony growth may be visible on underside of the leaf

text: Turn a leaf over: is there a velvety olive-green to brown mold under pale yellow or green patches on the top side?

passages.passage: On the underside, a velvety olive-green to brown mold develops.
Leaf mold begins as pale green or yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces

text: Do the spots look wet, dark and greasy, spreading quickly into big irregular brown-black patches?

passages.passage: When the weather is very humid and wet, late blight infections can appear water-soaked or dark brown in color, and are often described as appearing greasy.
The first symptoms of late blight on tomato leaves are irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions, often with a lighter halo or ring around them

text: Did the problem start on the oldest, lowest leaves near the soil and creep upward?

passages.passage: The leaf blight phase usually begins on the lower, older leaves and progresses up the plant.
it most commonly is found on the lower leaves.
these lesions are typically found on the younger, more succulent leaves in the top portion of the plant canopy

text: Do any tomatoes have small, raised, scabby brown spots, sometimes with a pale halo?

passages.passage: Fruit spots are 1/4 inch, slightly raised, brown and scabby. Tomato fruit often have a waxy white halo surrounding the fruit spot.

text: Do any green or ripening tomatoes have large, firm, sunken, greasy-looking brown patches?

passages.passage: Symptomatic tomato fruits appear mottled, often with golden to dark brown, firm, sunken surfaces.
Rotted fruit are typically firm with greasy spots that eventually become leathery and chocolate brown in color

text: Are there dark, elongated spots or cankers on the stems?

passages.passage: Early Blight produces a wide range of symptoms at all stages of plant growth: the most common are stem cankers, leaf spots, and fruit rot.
Stem and petiole lesions are brown and are typically not well defined in shape.

text: Is the fruit clean and unmarked even though the leaves are badly affected?

passages.passage: Leaf mold only affects tomato leaves. While fruit are not affected, yield losses may occur when leaf loss is severe.
Septoria, which rarely impacts stems or fruit directly.

text: Is each brown spot circled by a yellow ring (halo)?

passages.passage: Tomato leaves have small (less than 1/8 inch), brown, circular spots surrounded by a yellow halo.
A yellow halo usually surrounds the lesions.

text: On the top side of the leaf, are there pale green or yellow patches without a dark brown border?

passages.passage: Leaf mold begins as pale green or yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
Mature lesions have a dark margin with a grayish white center

text: Has the weather been very wet and humid or cool and foggy lately, or are the plants in a closed greenhouse or tunnel?

passages.passage: The production of pathogen spores is promoted by moist conditions (90–100% relative humidity) with moderate temperatures (60–80˚F).
Tomato leaf mold is caused by the non-obligate fungus Passalora fulva that thrives in conditions with humidity above 85% and temperatures between 68–77°F, commonly found in high tunnels.

text: When you shake the plant, do tiny white flying insects (whiteflies) fly up?

passages.passage: TYLCV is transmitted by adult whiteflies and is difficult to control once introduced to an area.
TMV and ToMV can be spread by tools, hands, and clothing.

text: Are the new leaves small, curled upward or cupped, crumpled and yellow along the edges and between the veins?

passages.passage: Leaves of infected plants are small and curl upward; and show strong crumpling and interveinal and marginal yellowing.
the primary symptoms of TYLCV are interveinal and marginal chlorosis of young leaves

text: Are the leaves mottled in patches of light and dark green, with raised dark green bumps, or narrow stringy fern-like leaflets?

passages.passage: Leaves may be mottled yellow and dark green. This is the symptom which gives the disease the name “mosaic.” The dark green areas may be raised.
Severely affected leaves may have a “fern- like” appearance and may show raised dark green areas.

text: Is the whole plant stunted and bushy, with short gaps between the leaves and flowers dropping off before fruit forms?

passages.passage: Plants infected with TYLCV will also be stunted in height ( Figure 3 ), and appear bushy due to shortened internode length. Flower drop will occur

text: Are there no spots or dead patches at all on the leaves, only yellowing, curling or mottling?

passages.passage: the primary symptoms of TYLCV are interveinal and marginal chlorosis of young leaves ( Figure 2 ), an overall crumpled appearance of the leaves, and upward and downward leaf-curling.
Leaves show green mottling and may be curled, stunted, and slightly deformed.
Tomato leaves have small (less than 1/8 inch), brown, circular spots surrounded by a yellow halo.

text: Does the whole plant look normal: evenly green leaves, no spots, curling or mottling, and normal growth?

passages.passage: Infected tomato plants initially show stunted and erect or upright plant growth; plants infected at an early stage of growth will show severe stunting.
Plants may be stunted and are generally somewhat yellowed.
Heavily diseased leaves turn yellow, wither, and drop in large numbers, starting at the base of the plant.

text: Are the spots angular, stopped by the leaf veins, with dark rings like a target inside?

passages.passage: Unlike late blight lesions, they are angular and become restricted by leaf veins.
lesion develop- ment is characterized by a series of dark concentric rings alternating with bands of light tan tissue

text: Turn a spotted leaf over: is there white or gray fuzzy growth around the edge of the spots on the underside?

passages.passage: Enlarged, water- soaked or wet and oily-appearing leaf lesions often give rise to sporulation, identifiable by white or gray fuzzy growth.
shows white, fuzzy, prolific pathogen sporulation in association with the brown lesion

text: Are the first spots on the oldest, lowest leaves, while the young leaves at the top are still clean?

passages.passage: Foliar symptoms of early blight ﬁ rst appear as small, irregular to circular dark brown spots on the lower (older) leaves.
On very young leaves, irregular, water-soaked lesions appear.

text: Did the spots appear after a spell of wet weather, looking dark, oily and water-soaked with a pale green halo, and growing fast?

passages.passage: The disease often appears following periods of very wet weather.
Lesions are dark brown to black, and can appear small at first. A light green halo often appears around the lesion.

text: If you cut into an affected tuber, is the flesh under the skin reddish-brown and granular, like rust?

passages.passage: Upon peeling back tuber epidermis (skin), reddish-brown to dark brown, granular tissue is apparent.

text: Are there dark, water-soaked streaks on the stems?

passages.passage: Dark green, brown, or black water-soaked lesions on the stem may also contain sporulation.
Elongated, superﬁ cial brown or black lesions may also form on stems and petioles.

text: Are the lesions long, narrow and rectangular, with straight sides that stop at the leaf veins?

passages.passage: Mature lesions are pale brown or gray to tan, long (0.2 to 2.0 inches), narrow and rectangular, being characteristically restricted by the veins

text: Are the lesions big, cigar-shaped patches, 1 to 6 inches long, tapering at both ends and running across the veins?

passages.passage: Mature lesions that characterize NCLB are elliptical (cigar-shaped), run parallel to the leaf margins, and are not restricted by leaf veins
The characteristic symptom of northern corn leaf blight on a susceptible hybrid is one-to-six inch long cigar-shaped gray- to tan-colored lesions on the leaves

text: Are there raised, powdery reddish-brown bumps that break through the leaf surface and rub off as rusty dust?

passages.passage: These lesions rapidly develop into oval to elongate shaped reddish-brown and powdery pustules that break through the surface giving the leaf a bumpy appearance.
Symptoms of common rust are elongate to oval brown pustules on both leaf surfaces which rupture and release red spores

text: Are the bumps or spots on both the top and the underside of the leaf?

passages.passage: Dark, reddish-brown pustules scattered over both the upper and lower surfaces of the corn leaves

text: Do the lesions have a dark gray or greenish dusty look in the middle, giving them a dirty appearance?

passages.passage: often have dark-gray to greenish, dusty masses of fungal spores in the center of the lesion, giving it a dirty appearance

text: Hold a leaf up to the light: do the small early spots have a yellow halo around them?

passages.passage: A yellow halo surrounding a small lesion is visible when the leaf is held up to light

text: Did the damage start on the lower leaves, well before the plants began to silk?

passages.passage: the disease is usually first noticed attacking the lower leaves well before silking

text: Are the leaves so covered in lesions that they look grayish-green and brittle, like frost-killed leaves?

passages.passage: The leaves then become grayish-green and brittle, resembling leaves killed by frost.

text: Are there velvety olive-green to brown patches on the leaf, with soft, feathery-looking edges?

passages.passage: Young lesions are velvety brown to olive green and have feathery, indistinct margins

text: Are there bright orange or yellow-orange spots on the top of the leaves, sometimes with a red or yellow border?

passages.passage: The most conspicuous symptoms of Cedar Apple Rust (CAR) on apple are bright orange lesions on the leaves. Lesions may have red or yellow borders.

text: Are there round spots with a light brown or gray center, dark brown rings around it and a purple edge, like a frog's eye?

passages.passage: The round to irregularly lobed spots develop a light brown-to-gray center surrounded by one or more dark-brown concentric rings and a purple margin giving it a “frogeye” appearance.

text: Are some leaves curled, puckered or shrunken out of shape around the spots?

passages.passage: Young leaves may become curled, dwarfed, and distorted when infections are numerous.

text: Turn an orange-spotted leaf over: are there small tube-like or hair-like projections on the underside?

passages.passage: One to two months later, lesions appear on the undersides of the leaves. These lesions bear small, tubular protrusions (aecia)

text: Is there a juniper or red cedar tree nearby with brown, round, golf-ball-like galls on it?

passages.passage: On eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginianae) cedar-apple rust produces brown, globular galls ranging in size from ¼” to 2 inches in diameter.

text: Are any apples rotting from the blossom end with brown rings, turning black and hard?

passages.passage: The disease usually starts at the calyx end of the fruit.
The rotted fruit finally turns black.

text: Are there rough, brown, corky scabs on the apples, or apples that are lopsided?

passages.passage: as the infected fruit enlarge, the lesions become brown and corky

text: Did the first spots show on the underside of the new leaves in a cool, wet spring, right after the buds opened?

passages.passage: The first lesions often occur on the lower surfaces of leaves as the leaves emerge and are exposed to infection in the spring.
Starting at petal-fall or somewhat later, small, purple specks appear on infected leaves.

text: Are the leaves evenly green, with no spots, blotches or twisted shapes anywhere on the tree?

passages.passage: Young lesions are velvety brown to olive green and have feathery, indistinct margins
The most conspicuous symptoms of Cedar Apple Rust (CAR) on apple are bright orange lesions on the leaves.
Starting at petal-fall or somewhat later, small, purple specks appear on infected leaves.

text: Are there small spots that began water-soaked on the underside of the leaf, then turned tan to brown and slightly greasy?

passages.passage: On leaves, the first symptoms are water-soaked spots visible on the lower leaf surface within 3 to 4 days of infection.
the lesions become tan to brown and appear slightly greasy on the upper leaf surface

text: Are the leaf edges scorched or are leaves dropping early?

passages.passage: Leaf margins may become scorched due to bacterial invasion of hydathodes. Infected leaves often drop prematurely

text: Do any peppers have raised, wart-like or scabby brown spots?

passages.passage: Fruit lesions enlarge, turn brown to black, and appear as raised warts or scabs

text: Has it been warm and humid with frequent rain or overhead watering, or did the seedlings come from a source that had spots?

passages.passage: All strains prefer high temperatures (75°F to 86°F), high humidity, and frequent rainfall/overhead irrigation.
The bacteria are seedborne, and outbreaks of the disease can occur within transplant production.

text: Are the leaves evenly green with no spots or yellow-brown patches, and the fruit smooth?

passages.passage: Leaf lesions expand and coalesce to form large areas of yellow and brown tissue with a characteristic greasy appearance
Lesions on fruit appear initially as small, raised blemishes that are a slightly lighter green than the normal fruit color.

text: Are there small tan circular spots, about 2 to 10 mm across, each with a dark brown border?

passages.passage: Leaf lesions ar e small (2 to 10 mm in diameter), tan and circular with a dark brown border.

text: Do the tan spots have tiny black specks in them?

passages.passage: Pycnidia: tiny black spore-producing bodies that often develop in lesions.

text: Have any berries shriveled into hard, black, dried-up mummies?

passages.passage: Within days of infection, the berry shrivels and dries into a hard, black mummy.

text: Are the leaves evenly green with no spots anywhere, and the berries plump and normal?

passages.passage: Leaf lesions ar e small (2 to 10 mm in diameter), tan and circular with a dark brown border.
Within days of infection, the berry shrivels and dries into a hard, black mummy.
